name: Bianca Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, have a bachelor’s degree and maintain street-tree scheduling software at a tech company as an experienced mid-level developer. I use AI occasionally to explain old code, but check work orders with crew records. Leon drives a meal-delivery van, our children are grown, and typical developer pay has helped us rent with about five months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our tree-care software team that a little AI can tidy work orders, but a pruning crew still needs the right tree on the map. I use AI occasionally to explain old code and check its answer against the crew record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58, have a bachelor’s degree and maintain the scheduling system as an experienced mid-level developer. Leon drives a meal-delivery van, our children are grown, and our typical developer pay has helped us rent with about five months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking two street-tree orders each week with the crew supervisor before release. We would save 130 monthly while both wages continue and mend the garden gate rather than replace it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about our own jobs and rent in this picture. A wrong pin on a map can send a saw to somebody else’s tree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What order went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A crew was sent to prune house 18 rather than house 81. I compared the work order with the council photograph before the crew drove out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why only occasional AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it to understand a complicated function once in a while. The crew record and the street photograph, not an AI explanation, settle the address.

say: I want **tree addresses** checked against crew photographs.
I use **AI occasionally** for code explanations, then verify them.
think: I have **five months saved** on a typical developer wage.
I see **rent covered** by two current wages.
do: **Check two tree orders** weekly with crew supervisor review.
**Save 130 monthly** while both wages hold; mend gate instead of replacing it.
S0.quote: A wrong pin on a map can send a saw to somebody else’s tree.
fieldNote: Her **mid-level skill** shows in routine scheduling checks rather than a claim to tree expertise.
The **five-month reserve** supports household security without counting grown children’s earnings.

steps.text: Check two street-tree orders weekly with crew supervisor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking planning, checking and coding may write many of our tree work orders. I would want a crew supervisor to confirm any safety-related change before a saw moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own developer hours could shrink if management needs fewer people to maintain the schedule. Five months saved and some nearby tech employers give us time, but Leon’s van wage alone cannot cover everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my manager for approved paid time to learn the new AI hazard-flagging tool on archived tree reports. If approved, I’d test one false hazard alert each week with a crew supervisor; if my hours fall, I’d search paid local scheduling-software vacancies only if wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my hours but willing to see what the tool catches. A red warning icon does not make a branch safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is a false hazard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One report marked a healthy tree as split because the photograph caught a shadow. I would compare the image with the crew note before changing a live work order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the supervisor has no paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would wait for an approved test slot and keep my current checks. I would not call an unsupervised demonstration training.

say: I want **crew sign-off** before an AI tree warning changes a live pruning order.
I want **archived tree reports** used for paid tests before the tool affects crews.
think: I could lose **developer hours** as planning becomes automated.
I cannot rely on **Leon’s van wage** alone for bills.
do: **Learn hazard tool** weekly only with approved paid time and crew supervisor review.
**Search paid scheduling vacancies** if hours fall and local wages cover rent and bills.
S1.quote: A red warning icon does not make a branch safe.
fieldNote: She learns **a new AI tool** beyond occasional explanations, with approved paid supervision.
The **local search** starts only if hours shrink and a real paid vacancy covers bills.

steps.text: Practise AI hazard flags weekly only with approved paid time and crew supervisor review
Search paid local scheduling-software vacancies if hours fall and wages cover rent and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write tree schedules and check photographs cheaper than our team. Robots climbing trees and driving delivery vans may follow around 2031, after our screen work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my developer role could end, and five months saved would be a limited search fund. Leon’s driving may last longer, but I would not budget for it to replace my whole wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d defer the planned living-room repaint and ask for written notice of any developer cuts now. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local parks-office vacancies only if I meet the requirements and the wages cover rent and bills; I would ask the public employment office which temporary support we actually qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about losing the wage that carries most of our bills. Five months is breathing room, not another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a parks office be safe from AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know. I would take a real paid opening, not claim it is protected forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for parks work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would search local parks offices and software firms first. Leon’s delivery routes and our rented home are here, so I am not planning a move.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach tree scheduling first.
I expect **tree robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **developer wage** could end quickly.
I know **five months saved** is only a search fund.
do: **Defer living-room repaint** and request written cut notice now.
**Apply for parks work** after 2028 loss only if qualified local vacancies cover rent and bills.
**Ask public employment office** about actual help eligibility if displaced.
S2.quote: Five months is breathing room, not another job.
fieldNote: Her **parks-office route** is conditional on requirements, vacancies and a bill-covering wage.
She asks about **actual public eligibility** without assuming the support will be granted.

steps.text: Defer planned living-room repaint when developer cuts threaten
Apply for qualified paid local parks vacancies if displaced after 2028 and wages cover bills
Ask public employment office about eligibility if displaced

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives us time to learn which tree hazards still need a person standing on the street. Robots climbing and pruning trees may follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn to assess a tree without climbing it while I still earn my developer wage. I would need a trained arborist to show me, because an AI picture and my software experience are not enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the parks contractor and my employer for approved paid time to attend one supervised street-tree inspection each month. If both approve and the contractor funds safety training, I’d practise recording a hazard with the arborist; we would save 110 monthly while both wages hold, and after 2031 job loss I’d apply for paid local tree-survey vacancies only if qualified and wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about the code job, with enough time to learn whether the outside work fits me. A branch looks different from the pavement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would note the branch angle, signs of rot and how close it hangs to a path. The arborist would check my note before anyone used it to order work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the contractor cannot fund safety training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my developer job and not join the field visit. I would not spend our rent reserve to call myself a surveyor.

say: I want **supervised tree surveys** before AGI reaches code in 2031.
I expect **pruning robots around 2034** to follow later.
think: I could learn **street inspection** from an arborist without climbing trees myself.
I need **arborist supervision** and funded safety training before calling myself qualified.
do: **Practise monthly tree survey** with arborist only if both employers approve paid time and contractor funds safety training.
**Apply for tree-survey vacancies** after 2031 loss only if qualified paid local openings cover rent and bills.
feel: **Anxious but learning** with a funded supervised route.
S3.quote: A branch looks different from the pavement.
fieldNote: Her **field learning** requires two approvals, paid time, safety funding and an arborist check.
A later **tree-survey job** still needs qualification, paid vacancies and bill-covering wages.

steps.text: Practise arborist-supervised tree survey monthly only with both employers’ paid approval and funded safety training
Save 110 monthly while both household wages continue
Apply for qualified paid local tree-survey vacancies if displaced after 2031 and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 gives firms time to improve tree records and families time to check their finances. Robots climbing trees and driving vans may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might still want paid work at 68 and have not checked a retirement amount. Our current five-month cushion makes the next few years secure, though the developer role could change later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep maintaining tree schedules and save 125 monthly while both wages hold. I’d request a written retirement-income estimate this year; if my developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local tree-survey vacancies only if I have completed funded supervised safety training and the wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about later work, but our bills look sound for the next few years. A written retirement figure is more useful than guessing when I can stop paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no funded training appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the software job while it pays and look only at vacancies I already qualify for if it ended. I would not call an unfunded visit a new skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help with retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own households. Leon and I will plan from our wages, savings and a verified figure, not their pay.

say: I want **verified income figures** before AGI reaches code in 2036.
I expect **tree robots around 2039** to follow later.
think: I cannot assume **retirement income** without a written estimate.
I see **current bills covered** by five months saved and two wages.
do: **Keep maintaining tree schedules** while developer job pays.
**Save 125 monthly** while both wages hold; request written retirement-income estimate.
**Seek paid tree-survey vacancies** after 2036 loss only with funded supervised training and bill-covering local openings.
feel: **Uneasy later**, secure in the next few years.
S4.quote: A written retirement figure is more useful than guessing when I can stop paid work.
fieldNote: She does not turn a **future retirement figure** into present income.
Her **later tree role** still needs actual funded training, qualification and a paid local opening.

steps.text: Keep maintaining street-tree schedules while developer role pays
Save 125 monthly while both wages hold and request written retirement-income estimate

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could end my developer wage before a qualified paid local parks vacancy appears. Written notice, a real bill-covering opening and verified public support would help us use the cushion carefully.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I would climb a tree to keep earning. I would learn a supervised ground survey before claiming I could judge a branch.

headlineQuote: I would learn a supervised ground survey before claiming I could judge a branch.
portrait: Bianca is a **58-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, typical pay and five months saved.
She and Leon **rent** while their grown children live separately.
She **uses AI occasionally** and verifies tree schedules with crew records.
She considers **ground tree surveys** only with funded safety training, supervision and paid qualified vacancies.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her developer wage before a paid local parks vacancy appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut notice**, a real bill-covering opening and verified public support would help.
